Homology converts geometry into linear algebra. Cells become basis vectors,
boundaries become matrices, and holes emerge from kernels and quotient spaces.
This chapter develops only the algebra needed for that conversion.

::: {.callout-note title="A geometric dictionary for the algebra"}
The chapter can be read with one picture in mind: take a square assembled from
edges.

| Linear-algebra term | Topological meaning later |
|---|---|
| basis vector | one cell, such as one edge |
| vector | a selected collection of cells |
| linear map | an operation such as taking the boundary |
| kernel | chains whose boundary vanishes |
| image | chains produced as boundaries of higher cells |
| quotient | identify two cycles when they differ only by a filled boundary |
| dimension | the number of independent features |

The definitions below are general because the same algebra works in every
dimension, but each has a concrete role in this table.
:::

## Fields and vector spaces

::: {#def-vector-space name="Field and vector space"}
A **field** is a set in which addition, subtraction, multiplication, and
division by nonzero elements behave as expected. Familiar examples are
$\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb R$.

For computation, we will often use

$$
\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\},
$$

with arithmetic modulo $2$. In particular,

$$
1+1=0.
$$

A **vector space** $V$ over a field $\mathbb F$ is a set whose elements can be
added and multiplied by scalars from $\mathbb F$.

Over $\mathbb F_2$, a vector is a binary string, vector addition is
componentwise XOR, and every vector is its own additive inverse.
:::

If a complex has ordered edges $(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)$, the binary vector

$$
(1,0,1,1)
$$

means “select $e_1,e_3,e_4$.” Adding $(1,1,0,0)$ gives
$(0,1,1,1)$ because the repeated edge $e_1$ cancels. This is why formal
vector addition has a visible geometric interpretation.

## Spans, independence, and bases

Given vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_m\in V$, their span is

$$
\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}
=
\left\{
\sum_{i=1}^m a_iv_i:a_i\in\mathbb F
\right\}.
$$

The vectors are **linearly independent** if

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m a_iv_i=0
$$

forces every $a_i=0$. A **basis** is a linearly independent spanning set. The
number of elements in a finite basis is the **dimension** of the vector space.

Later, the $k$-cells of a complex will form a basis for a vector space $C_k$.
A chain is then a linear combination of cells.

## Linear maps and matrices

A function $T\colon V\to W$ is **linear** if

$$
T(av+bw)=aT(v)+bT(w)
$$

for all vectors $v,w$ and scalars $a,b$.

After choosing bases, $T$ is represented by a matrix $A$. Its $j$th column is
the coordinate vector of the image of the $j$th basis vector.

This convention matters for boundary matrices: columns correspond to cells in
the domain, rows correspond to their facets in the codomain.

## Kernel, image, and rank

The **kernel** of $T$ is

$$
\ker T=\{v\in V:T(v)=0\}.
$$

The **image** is

$$
\operatorname{im}T=\{T(v):v\in V\}.
$$

Both are vector subspaces. Their dimensions are the **nullity** and **rank** of
$T$, respectively.

For finite-dimensional $V$, the rank–nullity theorem states

$$
\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T.
$$

This identity will turn the definition of homology into a practical formula
for Betti numbers.

::: {#thm-rank-nullity name="Rank–nullity theorem"}
Let $T\colon V\to W$ be linear, where $V$ is finite-dimensional. Then

$$
\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ of $\ker T$ and extend it to a basis
$v_1,\ldots,v_r,v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n$ of $V$. We claim that
$T(v_{r+1}),\ldots,T(v_n)$ is a basis for $\operatorname{im}T$.

It spans the image because any $v\in V$ is a linear combination of the
$v_i$, and the first $r$ terms vanish under $T$. For independence, if
$\sum_{i=r+1}^n a_iT(v_i)=0$, then
$\sum_{i=r+1}^n a_iv_i\in\ker T$, so it is also a combination of
$v_1,\ldots,v_r$. Uniqueness of coordinates in the full basis forces all
$a_i=0$. Hence $\dim\operatorname{im}T=n-r$, and the formula follows.
:::

## Quotient spaces

Quotient spaces are usually the least familiar construction in this chapter.
The guiding operation is **declaring certain differences irrelevant**. In
clock arithmetic, for example, the hours $2$ and $14$ are treated as the same
because their difference is a multiple of $12$. In homology, two cycles are
treated as the same when their difference is the boundary of a filled region.

Suppose $W$ is a subspace of $V$. Two vectors $v,v'\in V$ are equivalent
modulo $W$ when

$$
v-v'\in W.
$$

The equivalence class of $v$ is the coset

$$
v+W=\{v+w:w\in W\}.
$$

The set of all cosets is the **quotient space** $V/W$.

Quotienting declares every vector in $W$ to be algebraically trivial. This is
exactly what homology needs: cycles that differ by the boundary of a
higher-dimensional cell should represent the same hole.

Concretely, suppose $z$ is the perimeter of a square and $\kappa$ is its
filled interior. Since $\partial\kappa=z$, adding $z$ to another cycle merely
adds the boundary of a filled cell. In the quotient used by homology, the two
cycles represent the same class. A quotient does not erase the vectors in the
larger space; it groups vectors into equivalence classes according to the
difference we have chosen to ignore.

If $V$ is finite-dimensional, then

$$
\dim(V/W)=\dim V-\dim W.
$$

::: {#prp-quotient-dimension name="Dimension of a quotient"}
If $V$ is finite-dimensional and $W\leq V$, then

$$
\dim(V/W)=\dim V-\dim W.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Choose a basis $w_1,\ldots,w_r$ of $W$ and extend it to a basis
$w_1,\ldots,w_r,v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n$ of $V$. The cosets
$v_{r+1}+W,\ldots,v_n+W$ span $V/W$ and are linearly independent there.
They therefore form a basis of $V/W$, which has dimension $n-r$.
:::

## Why $\mathbb F_2$ is convenient

Working over $\mathbb F_2$ removes orientation signs. A cell is either present
or absent from a chain. When the same face appears twice, it cancels:

$$
e+e=0.
$$

For example, two adjacent squares share an edge. Adding their boundaries
causes the shared edge to appear twice, so it vanishes. The resulting boundary
is the outer perimeter.

This makes the theory and implementation clean. Other coefficient fields can
detect information hidden by $\mathbb F_2$, but binary coefficients are an
excellent first model.

The thesis fixes $\mathbb F_2$ for six related reasons:

1. **Orientation independence.** Since $-1=1$ in characteristic two, the
   alternating signs in an oriented boundary formula disappear.
2. **Binary incidence matrices.** Boundary matrices contain only zeroes and
   ones and can be reduced using XOR.
3. **Chains as subsets.** A cell has coefficient either zero or one, so a
   chain is identified with the subset of cells that occur.
4. **Transparent cancellation.** Every codimension-two face in
   $\partial^2$ occurs twice, and $1+1=0$.
5. **Vector-space homology.** Homology is characterised by dimensions, making
   Betti numbers directly accessible by rank–nullity.
6. **Gaussian elimination.** Over a field, ordinary row reduction replaces
   the Smith normal form required for integral homology.

This is a choice of coefficients, not a theorem that $\mathbb F_2$ is always
best. Integral coefficients can detect torsion and retain orientation
information. Those phenomena matter in many topological spaces, but not for
the thesis's narrow task of counting components and planar loops in digital
images. The notation $\mathbb F_2$ is used rather than $\mathbb Z_2$ to
emphasise the field structure and avoid confusion with the ring of
$2$-adic integers.

## Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb F_2$

Ranks and kernels are computed by row reduction. The legal operations are:

1. swap two rows;
2. add one row to another; and
3. omit rescaling, because the only nonzero scalar is $1$.

Addition is XOR, making binary elimination especially efficient.

Consider

$$
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&0\\
1&0&1\\
0&1&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this matrix has rank $3$. Over $\mathbb F_2$, the third row is
the sum of the first two, so its rank is $2$. Coefficients matter.

## Direct sums

This short section is a look ahead. Direct sums become important only when a
persistence module is decomposed into independent feature lifespans.

The **direct sum** $V\oplus W$ consists of pairs $(v,w)$ with componentwise
operations. Dimensions add:

$$
\dim(V\oplus W)=\dim V+\dim W.
$$

Persistent homology uses direct sums to decompose a complicated evolving
vector space into independent interval modules, one for each birth–death
interval.

## The algebraic destination

For boundary maps

$$
C_{k+1}\xrightarrow{\partial_{k+1}}
C_k\xrightarrow{\partial_k}C_{k-1},
$$

the identity $\partial_k\partial_{k+1}=0$ implies

$$
\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}
\subseteq
\ker\partial_k.
$$

Therefore, the quotient

$$
H_k=
\ker\partial_k/
\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}
$$

is well-defined. Its dimension is the $k$th Betti number.

::: {.callout-tip title="What to carry forward"}
The expression

$$
H_k=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}
$$

says: begin with every $k$-dimensional chain whose boundary vanishes, then
identify chains that differ by the boundary of a filled
$(k+1)$-dimensional chain. The next chapter constructs these two spaces
geometrically. If quotient notation still feels unfamiliar, this verbal
reading is sufficient to proceed.
:::

## Exercises

1. List all vectors in $\mathbb F_2^3$.
2. Find a basis for the span of $(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$ over $\mathbb F_2$.
3. Row-reduce the matrix $A$ above over $\mathbb F_2$.
4. If $\dim V=8$ and $\dim W=3$, compute $\dim(V/W)$.
5. Explain geometrically why shared edges cancel when adding two square
   boundaries over $\mathbb F_2$.
